title: Linux+ V8 (XK0-006) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public XK0-006 exam objectives. Not real exam questions. Practice on your own lab machines (WSL, a VM or a cloud sandbox), never on production systems you don't manage.

q.q: After a kernel update, a server shows the GRUB menu and starts loading the new kernel, then stops with "Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs". The old kernel still boots fine. What is the most likely cause?
o: The new kernel's initramfs lacks the storage driver

Right. The initramfs (initrd) loads the drivers the kernel needs to find the root disk. If it wasn't built for the new kernel, the root filesystem can't be mounted. Rebuild it (dracut or update-initramfs) from the old kernel.
The default systemd target was changed to rescue.target
systemd hasn't started yet when this panic happens; the kernel can't even mount root.
A typo in the /home line of /etc/fstab
fstab is read after the root filesystem is mounted, and a bad /home line leads to emergency mode, not a kernel panic.
GRUB is no longer installed in the disk's boot sector
The GRUB menu appeared and loaded the kernel, so the bootloader works.

q.q: An admin compiled a small monitoring tool from source. It isn't part of any package. Following the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, where should its binary go so the package manager never overwrites it?
o: /usr/local/bin
Right. /usr/local is for software the local admin installs outside the package manager.
/var/lib/bin
/var/lib holds variable state data for programs, like databases, not executables.
/boot/bin
/boot holds the kernel, initramfs and bootloader files only.
/usr/bin
/usr/bin belongs to the package manager; a later package could overwrite or conflict with the file.

q.q: A company changes the code of a GPLv3-licensed tool and ships the changed program to its customers. What does the license require?
o: Publish only the original unmodified source, keeping the company's changes private
The obligation covers the modified code that was distributed, not just the original.
Pay a per-copy royalty to the original authors instead of sharing code
The GPL charges no royalties; its condition is sharing source.
Give those customers the changed source code under the same GPL terms
Right. The GPL is copyleft: anyone who distributes a modified version must share its source under the same license.
Nothing, because the changes make it the company's own proprietary product
Copyleft exists exactly to stop modified versions from becoming closed.

q.q: A vendor's monitoring agent installs fine on the team's older servers, but on a new server the install fails with "package architecture (amd64) does not match system (arm64)". What explains this?
o: The agent must be converted with alien from .deb to .rpm first
alien converts package formats, not CPU architectures; the message is about the CPU.
The package needs to be installed with a GUI package manager on newer releases
The tool used to install doesn't change the binary's architecture.
The new server has an ARM CPU, so it needs an arm64 (aarch64) build of the agent
Right. Binaries are compiled for one CPU architecture. uname -m shows aarch64 on ARM servers; get the package built for it.
The new server runs a different Linux kernel version than the old servers
A different kernel version doesn't change the CPU architecture a binary is built for.

q.q: An admin needs to load the kernel module for a new network card. The module depends on two other modules that aren't loaded yet. Which command loads it and its dependencies in one step?
o: lsmod
lsmod only lists modules that are already loaded.
modprobe
Right. modprobe reads modules.dep and loads the dependencies first.
depmod
depmod builds the dependency list that modprobe uses; it doesn't load anything.
insmod
insmod loads one .ko file from a path and doesn't resolve dependencies, so it fails here.

q.q: A vendor gives you mydrv.ko. You copy it to /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/extra/, but "modprobe mydrv" says "Module mydrv not found". What should you run next?
o: modinfo -F depends mydrv to load its dependencies
modinfo shows information about a module; it never loads anything.
lsmod | grep mydrv to confirm it's loaded
It isn't loaded; lsmod won't change that.
depmod -a, then modprobe mydrv again
Right. modprobe finds modules through modules.dep. depmod -a rebuilds it so the new file is known.
Add mydrv to /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist.conf and reboot
A blacklist stops a module from loading; that's the opposite of what you want.

q.q: The open-source nouveau graphics driver keeps loading at boot and conflicts with the vendor driver. What stops it from loading at every boot?
o: Add "blacklist nouveau" to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ and rebuild the initramfs
Right. A blacklist line stops automatic loading. Rebuilding the initramfs matters because the driver may also be loaded from there early in boot.
Run rmmod nouveau once from a root shell
rmmod unloads it now, but it comes back at the next boot.
Add nouveau to a file in /etc/modules-load.d/ so systemd manages it at boot
Files there list modules to load at boot, which is the opposite.
Run modinfo nouveau and delete the parameters it lists
modinfo only displays information about the module.

q.q: A USB GPS receiver shows up as /dev/ttyUSB0 on some boots and /dev/ttyUSB1 on others, breaking the app that reads it. What is the best fix?
o: Create /dev/gps by hand with mknod during installation
/dev is rebuilt by udev at every boot, so a hand-made node disappears.
Load the usbserial module with modprobe and a fixed port option
Module options don't decide the order devices are named.
Mount /dev/ttyUSB0 at /dev/gps with an fstab entry using defaults,nofail
A serial device has no filesystem to mount; fstab doesn't apply.
A udev rule that matches its serial number and adds a /dev/gps symlink
Right. udev creates /dev entries as devices appear. A rule matched on a stable attribute gives the app a name that never changes.

q.q: The /var logical volume (ext4) is full. Its volume group has 20 GiB free. Which single command adds 10 GiB to /var while it stays mounted?
o: mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg0/var after extending it
mkfs creates a new empty filesystem and destroys the data on /var.
lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vg0/var
Right. -L +10G grows the logical volume and -r resizes the filesystem on it right after, online.
vgextend vg0 /dev/vg0/var
vgextend adds a physical volume to a VG. The VG already has free space; the LV needs to grow.
lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/var, with nothing else
The LV grows, but the filesystem doesn't, so df still shows the old size until you resize it.

q.q: A team asks you to shrink the XFS filesystem on /data from 500 GiB to 300 GiB to free space in the volume group. What is the correct plan?
o: xfs_growfs -D with a smaller block count
xfs_growfs only grows; it refuses a smaller size.
Back up, recreate it smaller, then restore the data
Right. XFS can grow but can never shrink. The only way down is back up, recreate and restore.
resize2fs /dev/vg0/data 300G after unmounting
resize2fs is for ext2/3/4, not XFS.
lvreduce -r -L 300G /dev/vg0/data while it is mounted
lvreduce -r needs a filesystem that can shrink; XFS can't, so the resize fails.

q.q: A server mounts an NFS share from /etc/fstab. When the NAS is down, the server hangs at boot. Which change lets boot continue without the share?
o: Add noexec to the share's mount options
noexec blocks running programs from the share; it doesn't affect failed mounts.
Replace the NAS hostname with its IP address
The NAS is down, so the IP won't answer either.
Add nofail (and _netdev) to the share's mount options
Right. nofail tells systemd not to block boot if the mount fails; _netdev marks it as needing the network.
Set the share's sixth fstab field (fsck order) to 2
That field controls fsck order for local disks, not network mount failures.

q.q: A server has four disks. The data must survive any two disks failing at the same time. Which RAID level fits?
o: RAID 10
RAID 10 survives two failures only if they are in different mirror pairs, not any two.
RAID 6
Right. RAID 6 keeps two sets of parity, so any two disks can fail.
RAID 0
RAID 0 has no redundancy; one failed disk loses everything.
RAID 5
RAID 5 has one parity set and survives only one failed disk.

q.q: Why do admins put UUID=... in /etc/fstab instead of names like /dev/sdb1?
o: ext4 and XFS refuse to mount from a /dev name in fstab
Device names still work; they just aren't stable.
UUIDs hide the disk layout from non-root users
UUIDs are visible with blkid and lsblk; it isn't a security feature.
Device names can change; UUIDs stay with the filesystem
Right. The UUID belongs to the filesystem, so it still points to the right one if sdb becomes sdc.
UUIDs mount faster because the kernel skips the device scan
Mount speed is the same; the benefit is a stable name.

q.q: "dig app01.corp.local" returns 10.0.5.20, the correct address. But "ping app01.corp.local" tries 10.0.9.9, the server's old address. What is the most likely cause?
o: The wrong DNS server is listed in /etc/resolv.conf
dig used the same resolv.conf and got the right answer, so DNS is fine.
The host firewall is rewriting ICMP packets to the old address
Firewalls don't change name resolution results.
The DNS record's TTL hasn't expired on the authoritative server
dig already returns the new address, so the record is current.
A stale /etc/hosts entry that's checked before DNS
Right. dig asks DNS directly. ping uses the system resolver, which follows nsswitch.conf and checks /etc/hosts first.

q.q: On a RHEL server using NetworkManager, you need eth0 to keep the static address 10.1.1.5/24 after reboots. Which approach works?
o: ip addr add 10.1.1.5/24 dev eth0
ip changes are live only and disappear at the next reboot or reconnect.
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 10.1.1.5/24 ipv4.method manual, then nmcli con up eth0
Right. nmcli saves the change in the connection profile, so it survives reboots, and con up applies it now.
Add "address 10.1.1.5" to /etc/resolv.conf
resolv.conf lists DNS servers, not interface addresses.
ifconfig eth0 10.1.1.5 netmask 255.255.255.0 up
Like ip, ifconfig changes don't persist, and the tool is deprecated.

q.q: You're connected over SSH to an Ubuntu server and must change its Netplan YAML. If the change cuts off your connection, you want it to undo itself. Which command should you use?
o: netplan generate
It only writes the backend config files and doesn't apply or test anything.
netplan apply
It applies the change with no automatic rollback; a bad config locks you out.
nmcli connection reload
That reloads NetworkManager profiles; it has no rollback timer.
netplan try
Right. netplan try applies the config and rolls it back automatically unless you confirm within the timeout.

q.q: A port scan reports TCP 8443 open on a server, and you need to know which program is listening on it. Which command shows that?
o: dig -p 8443 localhost
dig is a DNS tool; -p only changes which port it sends DNS queries to.
ip route show
That shows the routing table, not sockets.
ss -tlnp
Right. -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric, -p shows the process name and PID (run it as root).
netstat -r
-r prints the routing table, not listening sockets.

q.q: You need to capture only DNS traffic on eth0 into a file to open later in Wireshark. Which command does that?
o: tcpdump -i eth0 -r dns.pcap port 53
-r reads an existing capture file instead of writing one.
dig +trace @eth0 > dns.pcap
dig sends its own queries; it doesn't capture other traffic.
tcpdump -i eth0 -A host 53 > dns.pcap
"host 53" filters on an IP address, and -A prints text, not a pcap file.
tcpdump -i eth0 -w dns.pcap port 53
Right. -w writes raw packets to a file and the filter "port 53" keeps only DNS.

q.q: You want the list of .conf files that find locates saved in confs.txt, and the "Permission denied" errors thrown away. Which command does that?
o: find / -name '*.conf' 2>/dev/null > confs.txt
Right. 2> sends errors (stream 2) to /dev/null and > sends normal output (stream 1) to the file.
find / -name '*.conf' &> confs.txt
&> sends both output and errors into the file.
find / -name '*.conf' > /dev/null 2> confs.txt
This is backwards: results are thrown away and only errors are saved.
find / -name '*.conf' > confs.txt 2>&1
2>&1 sends errors to the same place as output, so they end up in the file.

q.q:
Lines in auth.log look like:
Nov 18 03:12:44 web1 sshd[811]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4422 ssh2
Which pipeline counts failed logins per IP, highest first?
o: grep -c 'Failed password' auth.log | sort -rn
grep -c prints one total for the whole file, not a count per IP.
grep 'Failed password' auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | uniq -c | sort -rn
uniq only merges duplicates that sit next to each other. Without sort first, one IP is split into many small counts.
grep 'Failed password' auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Right. awk prints the 4th field from the end (the IP), sort groups matching IPs together, uniq -c counts them and sort -rn puts the biggest count first.
grep 'Failed password' auth.log | sort -rn | uniq -c
Every whole line is unique (times and ports differ), so each count is 1.

q.q: /opt/tools/bin/report runs with its full path, but typing "report" gives "command not found". How do you fix this for your user in all future shells?
o: Add the line "/opt/tools/bin report" to /etc/hosts
/etc/hosts maps names to IP addresses, not commands.
Run export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tools/bin" at the prompt
That works only in the current shell; it's gone when you log out.
Add export PATH="/opt/tools/bin" to ~/.bashrc
That replaces PATH, so ls, grep and other commands stop being found.
Add export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tools/bin" to ~/.bashrc
Right. Appending to PATH in a startup file keeps the existing directories and adds the new one in every new shell.

q.q: You need to change "PermitRootLogin yes" to "PermitRootLogin no" directly in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Which command edits the file in place?
o: sed -n 's/^PermitRootLogin yes/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
-n hides output and doesn't edit the file, so nothing visible happens.
sed -i 's/^PermitRootLogin yes/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Right. -i writes the change back to the file; ^ anchors the match to the start of the line.
grep -v 'PermitRootLogin yes' sshd_config > sshd_config
The shell empties the file before grep reads it, so you lose the whole config.
sed 's/^PermitRootLogin yes/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Without -i, sed prints the changed text to the screen and leaves the file alone.

q.q:
As a regular user with sudo rights, you run: sudo echo "10.0.5.20 app01" >> /etc/hosts
You get "Permission denied". Why, and what works instead?
o: echo needs its own sudoers entry; add echo to /etc/sudoers
echo ran fine as root; the failure is the redirection done by your shell.
Your shell does the >> redirect, not sudo; pipe to sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
Right. Redirection happens in your unprivileged shell before sudo runs. tee runs as root, so it can append to the file.
You must use > instead of >> for root-owned files
Either operator is done by your shell and fails the same way; > would also erase the file.
/etc/hosts is immutable by default on most distros; run sudo chattr -i /etc/hosts first
hosts isn't immutable by default, and the error comes from the redirection.

q.q: Which command creates a gzip-compressed archive of /etc?
o: tar -cjf etc-backup.tar.gz /etc
-j uses bzip2, not gzip, despite the .gz name.
gzip -r /etc > etc-backup.tar.gz
gzip -r compresses each file in /etc in place, changing the live config files.
tar -czf etc-backup.tar.gz /etc
Right. -c create, -z gzip, -f names the archive file. tar stores owners and permissions in the archive; add -p when extracting (as root) to restore them exactly.
tar -xzf etc-backup.tar.gz /etc
-x extracts an archive; it doesn't create one.

q.q: Before restoring, you want to see which files are inside backup.tar.gz without extracting or changing anything. Which command?
o: tar -xvzf backup.tar.gz
-x extracts the files, which could overwrite current ones.
gunzip -l backup.tar.gz
That shows compressed and uncompressed sizes, not the files inside the tar.
tar -tzf backup.tar.gz
Right. -t lists the archive's contents.
tar -cvzf backup.tar.gz
-c creates an archive with that name, overwriting your backup.

q.q: Each night, /srv/www must be copied to a backup server over SSH. Only changed files should be sent, and files deleted at the source must also disappear from the copy. Which command fits?
o: rsync -az /srv/www/ backup01:/srv/www/
Without --delete, files removed from the source stay on the backup.
dd if=/srv/www of=backup01:/srv/www
dd copies raw devices or files, not directory trees, and can't write to a remote path.
scp -r /srv/www backup01:/srv/www
scp copies everything every time and never removes deleted files.
rsync -az --delete /srv/www/ backup01:/srv/www/
Right. rsync sends only differences over SSH; -a keeps permissions and times, -z compresses and --delete removes files gone from the source.

q.q: You need a full image of the disk /dev/sdb saved to /backup/sdb.img. Which command is correct?
o: tar -cf /backup/sdb.img /dev/sdb
tar archives the device node file itself, not the disk's contents.
cp -a /dev/sdb1 /backup/sdb.img
That copies one partition, not the whole disk with its partition table.
dd if=/backup/sdb.img of=/dev/sdb bs=4M status=progress
This is reversed: it writes the image over the disk, which is a restore.
dd if=/dev/sdb of=/backup/sdb.img bs=4M status=progress
Right. if is the input (the disk) and of is the output (the image file).

q.q: A KVM guest must get an address from the office DHCP server and be reachable by other office PCs like any physical machine. Which virtual network type fits?
o: Routed without any change to the LAN router
A routed network needs routes on the LAN pointing to the host, and the VM wouldn't use the office DHCP.
NAT
With NAT (libvirt's default) the VM hides behind the host's address and LAN PCs can't reach it directly.
Bridged
Right. A bridge connects the VM's NIC to the physical LAN, so it gets its own LAN address.
Isolated
An isolated network only connects VMs to each other.

q.q: "virsh list" shows only two VMs, but you know the host has five. How do you see all of them, including the stopped ones?
o: virt-install --list
virt-install creates new VMs; it doesn't list them.
qemu-img info /var/lib/libvirt/images
qemu-img inspects disk image files, not VM definitions.
virsh dominfo --all
dominfo shows details for one named VM and has no --all option.
virsh list --all
Right. Without --all, virsh list shows only running domains.

q.q: Before installing KVM on a physical server, how can you confirm that the CPU supports hardware virtualization?
o: uname -m prints x86_64
That shows a 64-bit CPU, not whether VT-x or AMD-V is there.
grep -cE 'vmx|svm' /proc/cpuinfo prints more than 0
Right. vmx (Intel VT-x) or svm (AMD-V) in the CPU flags means hardware virtualization is available. If it's 0, also check the firmware setting.
free -h shows at least 8 GiB of RAM available for guests
Memory size has nothing to do with CPU virtualization support.
systemctl status libvirtd shows active
libvirtd can run without hardware support and would fall back to slow emulation.

q.q: The VM "web01" should start automatically whenever the host boots. Which command sets that?
o: virsh define web01
define registers a VM from an XML file; it doesn't set autostart.
virsh autostart web01
Right. autostart marks the domain to start when libvirtd starts at boot.
systemctl enable web01
web01 is a libvirt domain, not a systemd unit.
virsh start web01
That starts it once, right now; it won't start after the next reboot.

q.q: app.conf has one hard link (app.hard) and one symbolic link (app.sym) pointing to it. An admin deletes app.conf. What happens?
o: Both links still open the data because the inode is kept until reboot
The symlink points to a name, not an inode; once the name is gone, the symlink dangles.
app.hard still opens the data; app.sym is now broken
Right. A hard link is another name for the same inode, so the data stays while any name remains. A symlink stores a path, and that path is gone.
Both links break, because deleting the original removes the inode and its data blocks
The inode stays while its link count is above zero, and app.hard still counts.
app.sym still works but app.hard breaks, since hard links copy only the file name
It's the other way around: hard links share the inode, symlinks hold a path.

q.q: Something changed a config file under /etc in the last day. Which command lists files under /etc modified in the last 24 hours?
o: find /etc -atime -1 -type f
-atime is last access (read) time, not modification.
find /etc -mtime +1
+1 means modified more than one full day ago, the opposite.
find /etc -mtime -1
Right. -mtime -1 means modified less than one day ago.
find /etc -mmin -1 -type f
-mmin -1 means the last minute, not the last day.

q.q: /var is filling up and you suspect a few huge files. Which command finds files larger than 1 GiB anywhere under /var?
o: find /var -type f -size +1G
Right. +1G means larger than 1 GiB.
find /var -type f -size 1G
Without +, find matches files of about exactly 1 GiB (rounded up), not larger.
ls -lS /var | head
ls -lS sorts only the top level of /var; it doesn't search subdirectories.
du -sh /var
That prints one total for /var, not which files are large.

q.q: A user downloaded report.pdf, but no PDF viewer opens it. Which command checks what kind of data the file really holds?
o: stat report.pdf
stat shows size, owner, permissions and times, not the file's content type.
ls -l report.pdf
ls shows permissions, owner and size, not what the data is.
file report.pdf
Right. file looks at the content (magic bytes), not the name. Attackers often hide other file types behind a trusted extension.
locate report.pdf
locate only finds where files with that name are stored.

q.q: ls -l /dev/sda shows "brw-rw---- 1 root disk 8, 0". What does the leading b mean?
o: Binary executable that the kernel can run directly
Executables are regular files (-) with x bits.
Broken symbolic link whose target was deleted
A symlink shows l, broken or not.
Block device: data moves in blocks, like a disk
Right. The first character is the file type: b is block, c is character, d is directory, l is symlink.
Character device that streams one byte at a time, like a terminal
That would show a c, not a b.

q.q: alice is in the groups wheel and devs. She also needs to be in docker. Which command adds docker without removing her other groups?
o: usermod -aG docker alice
Right. -a appends to her supplementary groups; without it, -G replaces the whole list.
usermod -G docker alice
Without -a, her supplementary groups become only docker, so she loses wheel and devs.
useradd -G docker alice
useradd creates accounts; alice already exists, so it fails.
groupadd docker alice
groupadd creates a new group; it doesn't add members.

q.q: In /etc/shadow, bob's line starts with "bob:!$6$Xk3...". What does the ! in front of the hash mean?
o: The account has expired and bob must ask an admin to reactivate it
Account expiry is stored in a later shadow field, not with ! in the hash.
bob must choose a new password the next time he logs in
Forced change is set with chage -d 0, which changes the last-change field.
bob has no password at all, so anyone can log in as him without typing one
An empty field would mean no password; ! means locked.
His password is locked, but SSH key logins may still work
Right. usermod -L or passwd -l adds ! so the hash can never match. Key-based SSH doesn't check the password, so also expire the account to fully block it.

q.q: A contractor's account must stop working on December 31, 2026. Which command sets that?
o: chage -E 2026-12-31 contractor
Right. -E sets the account expiration date; after it, the account can't log in.
chage -M 31 contractor
-M sets the maximum days between password changes, not an end date.
userdel -r contractor --date 2026-12-31
userdel has no date option; it deletes the account right away.
passwd -l contractor
That locks the password today, not on December 31.

q.q: Every new user's home directory should start with the company's standard .bashrc and a README. Where do you put those files?
o: /etc/default/useradd
That file sets useradd defaults like shell and home base; it isn't a folder of files to copy.
/etc/profile.d
Scripts there run at login for every user; they aren't copied into home directories.
/etc/skel
Right. useradd -m copies everything in /etc/skel into each new home directory.
/root
/root is root's own home directory.

q.q: A new app needs its own service account that can own files but must never be used for an interactive login. Which command fits best?
o: useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin appsvc
Right. -r makes a system account (low UID, no aging) and nologin refuses interactive logins.
useradd -r -s /bin/bash appsvc
It's a system account, but bash still allows interactive logins.
adduser appsvc, then give it a strong password
A strong password still leaves an interactive login open.
useradd -m -s /bin/bash appsvc
That creates a normal user with a login shell, which can log in once a password or key is set.

q.q: Which crontab line runs /usr/local/bin/backup.sh at 2:30 AM every Monday?
o: 30 2 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
Right. The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. 1 is Monday.
* 2 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
* in the minute field runs it every minute from 2:00 to 2:59 on Mondays.
2 30 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
Minute and hour are swapped, and 30 isn't a valid hour.
30 2 1 * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
That runs at 2:30 AM on the 1st of every month.

q.q: A report job uses a lot of CPU. You want to start it so it gets the least CPU time when others need it. Which command?
o: kill -STOP ./report.sh
That pauses a process (by PID) instead of lowering its priority.
nice -n 19 ./report.sh
Right. 19 is the lowest priority (the "nicest" to other processes).
nice -n -20 ./report.sh
-20 is the highest priority, and only root may set it.
renice -n 19 ./report.sh
renice changes a running process by PID; it doesn't start a program.

q.q: ps shows a process with STAT Z and <defunct>. kill -9 on its PID does nothing. What is going on?
o: It already exited; its parent hasn't read its exit status yet
Right. A zombie uses no CPU or memory, only a process table slot. Fix or restart the parent so it reaps the child.
It's a kernel thread, and those can only be stopped with a reboot
Kernel threads show in brackets with normal states, not as defunct.
It's using all the CPU and the kernel is protecting it from kill
A zombie isn't running at all and uses no CPU.
It's stuck waiting on disk I/O and will finish after the disk replies
That's state D (uninterruptible sleep), not Z.

q.q: You started a long copy in the foreground of your SSH session. You want your prompt back without restarting the copy. What do you do?
o: Press Ctrl+Z, then type bg
Right. Ctrl+Z suspends the job and bg continues it in the background.
Type fg, then press Enter twice to detach it
fg brings a job to the foreground; it doesn't release the prompt.
Type jobs -b while the copy is still running
You can't type commands while the copy holds the prompt, and jobs only lists jobs.
Press Ctrl+C, then run the same command again with & at the end
Ctrl+C kills the copy, so it starts over.

q.q: A one-time maintenance script must run at 17:00 today and never again. Which tool fits best?
o: sleep 17:00 && ./maint.sh in the current shell
sleep takes a duration, not a clock time, and it dies if you log out.
A crontab line with minute 0 and hour 17
cron repeats the job every day until you remove the line.
A systemd timer with OnBootSec=17h set in it
OnBootSec counts from boot, not a time of day, and timers are meant for repeats.
Right. at schedules a command to run once at a set time.

q.q: On a RHEL server, which command tells you which installed package owns /usr/bin/dig?
o: dpkg -S /usr/bin/dig
dpkg is the Debian tool; it won't work on RHEL.
rpm -qa dig
-qa lists installed packages by name; dig isn't a package name.
dnf list installed /usr/bin/dig
dnf list matches package names, not file paths.
rpm -qf /usr/bin/dig
Right. -q queries and -f asks which package a file belongs to. dnf provides works too.

q.q: On Ubuntu you downloaded tool_2.1_amd64.deb. It needs two libraries that aren't installed. Which command installs it and pulls the dependencies from the repos?
o: apt-get download tool_2.1_amd64.deb
download only fetches a package from a repo by name; it installs nothing.
apt install ./tool_2.1_amd64.deb
Right. apt installs a local .deb (the ./ matters) and resolves its dependencies from the repositories.
dpkg -i tool_2.1_amd64.deb
dpkg doesn't fetch dependencies; the install fails and leaves the package half-configured.
rpm -ivh tool_2.1_amd64.deb
rpm is for RPM packages on RHEL-family systems.

q.q: On a RHEL-family server, monthly updates must never upgrade the kernel until a vendor approves it. Other packages should update as usual. What does that?
o: dnf remove kernel, then reinstall it after approval
Removing the running kernel is risky and isn't how you hold a version.
Set enabled=0 for the BaseOS repo
That blocks updates for every package in that repo, not only the kernel.
apt-mark hold linux-image-generic
apt-mark is for Debian and Ubuntu, not dnf.
Add exclude=kernel* to /etc/dnf/dnf.conf
Right. dnf skips matching packages during updates. The versionlock plugin is another option.

q.q: Two Java versions are installed and /usr/bin/java points to the wrong one. How do you choose the system default the supported way?
o: export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21 in /etc/hosts
/etc/hosts maps names to IP addresses; it never sets variables.
update-alternatives --config java
Right. The alternatives system manages the /usr/bin/java symlink chain and lets you pick from a menu.
Remove the older Java package so only one is left
That works only by deleting software other apps may need.
ln -sf /usr/lib/jvm/java-21/bin/java /usr/bin/java
Overwriting the link by hand bypasses alternatives, and the next update can reset it.

q.q: What is the main reason to install a desktop app as a snap or flatpak instead of a normal distro package?
o: It skips the package signature checks, which makes installs simpler
Snap and Flatpak both verify signatures.
It bundles its own libraries and runs sandboxed
Right. Bundled dependencies let one package run on many distros and versions, and the sandbox limits what the app can reach.
It runs faster because it's compiled for your exact CPU model
Bundled apps usually start a bit slower, not faster.
It shares the distro's libraries, so the download is smaller
It's the opposite: bundling makes downloads larger.

q.q: You edited /etc/systemd/system/app.service and ran systemctl restart app. systemd warns that the unit file changed on disk and keeps using the old settings. What did you skip?
o: systemctl enable app
enable controls start at boot; it doesn't reload unit files.
journalctl --vacuum-time=1d
That trims old logs and has nothing to do with unit files.
systemctl daemon-reload
Right. systemd caches unit files; daemon-reload makes it reread them.
systemctl isolate app.service
isolate switches targets and stops other units; it doesn't reread files.

q.q: A legacy service must never start: not by hand, not at boot and not as another unit's dependency. Which command?
o: systemctl kill legacy.service
kill sends a signal to its processes now; it can start again later.
systemctl disable legacy.service
disable removes boot start, but someone or another unit can still start it.
systemctl mask legacy.service
Right. mask links the unit to /dev/null, so nothing can start it until it's unmasked.
systemctl stop legacy.service
stop only stops it now.

q.q: You need to change one setting (LimitNOFILE) for the nginx unit that came from the package. What is the right way, so updates don't undo it?
o: Copy the unit to /etc/init.d/ and edit the copy
/etc/init.d holds old SysV scripts; systemd units don't go there.
Run systemctl edit nginx to create a drop-in override
Right. A drop-in overrides only the lines you set and survives package updates.
Edit /usr/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service directly
Files under /usr/lib belong to the package and are replaced on update.
Put LimitNOFILE in /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and reload nginx
LimitNOFILE is a systemd unit setting; nginx's own config won't apply it.

q.q: Which command shows only error-level and worse messages from sshd since the last boot?
o: journalctl -u sshd -b -p err
Right. -u picks the unit, -b the current boot and -p err the priority err and above.
systemctl list-units --failed sshd
That lists units in failed state, not log messages.
journalctl -f -u sshd
-f follows new messages live at every priority; it doesn't filter errors.
dmesg | grep sshd
dmesg shows the kernel ring buffer; sshd's messages are in the journal.

q.q: A server boots to a graphical login, but it should boot to text mode from now on. Which command?
o: systemctl isolate multi-user.target
isolate switches now, but the next boot is graphical again.
systemctl set-default graphical.target
That keeps the graphical boot.
systemctl set-default multi-user.target
Right. set-default changes the target used at every boot.
Change id:5 to id:3 in /etc/inittab
inittab is SysV init; systemd ignores it.

q.q: A MariaDB container loses all its data every time it's removed and recreated from the image. What keeps the data?
o: Use docker restart instead of removing it so the layer is kept
That works only until the next real update, which needs a recreate.
Run docker commit after every change to save the data into the image
That bakes data into images; it's slow, messy and not how data is kept.
Mount a named volume at /var/lib/mysql
Right. A volume lives outside the container's writable layer, so it survives removal and recreation.
Give the container more memory so the database stops flushing
Memory doesn't decide where data is stored.

q.q: A web container listens on port 80 inside. Users must reach it on the host's port 8080. Which option?
o: Reversed: that maps host port 80 to container port 8080, where nothing listens.
Right. The format is host_port:container_port.
--expose 80
--expose only documents the port; it doesn't publish it on the host.
--network host -p 8080
With host networking the app uses the host's port 80 directly; -p is ignored.

q.q: What is the main security benefit of running containers with rootless Podman?
o: Containers can bind to port 80 without any extra settings
Unprivileged users can't bind ports below 1024 by default.
Images are scanned for vulnerabilities before they run
Podman doesn't scan images by itself; that's a separate tool.
There's no root daemon, so a breakout lands as a normal user
Right. Rootless containers map root in the container to a normal user on the host, which limits the damage of an escape.
Container traffic between hosts is encrypted automatically with TLS
Rootless mode doesn't add encryption.

q.q: A developer asks to run a container with --privileged to fix a "permission denied" error on a mounted folder. What is the best response?
o: Approve it, since containers are isolated whatever their flags
--privileged removes most of that isolation.
Refuse; fix the folder's ownership or SELinux label instead
Right. --privileged gives the container almost full access to the host's devices and kernel features. Grant the smallest thing that fixes it.
Approve it, but also run the app as root inside for safety
Running as root adds risk; it doesn't make --privileged safer.
Disable SELinux on the host so containers stop hitting labels
That weakens the whole host to fix one mount.

q.q: During a hardening review you need a list of every SUID file on the system. Which command finds them?
o: ls -la / | grep rws
That checks only the top of / and misses everything in subdirectories.
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
Right. -perm -4000 matches files with the SUID bit set. Attackers look for odd SUID binaries to escalate privileges.
find / -perm 777 -type f 2>/dev/null
That finds world-writable rwx files, not SUID.
find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null
2000 is the SGID bit, not SUID.

q.q: Help desk staff in the group helpdesk must be able to restart httpd, and nothing else, as root. What should you add with visudo?
o: chmod u+s /usr/bin/systemctl so they can run it as root
SUID on systemctl gives every user root control of every service.
%helpdesk ALL=(ALL) ALL
That gives them every command as any user, which is full root.
Add every helpdesk member to the wheel group
On RHEL, wheel members get full sudo, far more than restarting httpd.
%helpdesk ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart httpd
Right. % means a group, and listing the full command limits them to exactly that action.

q.q: The user auditor must be able to read everything in /srv/reports. You can't change the owner or group, and others must stay blocked. Which command fits?
o: chown -R auditor /srv/reports
That changes the owner, which you were told not to do.
chmod -R o+r /srv/reports
That lets every user on the system read the reports.
getfacl -R -m u:auditor:r /srv/reports
getfacl only shows ACLs; it can't change them.
setfacl -R -m u:auditor:rX /srv/reports
Right. An ACL adds one user's access without touching owner, group or other. X adds execute only on directories (so they can be opened).

q.q: An audit log file must allow new lines to be added but block edits and deletion, even by root, until an admin removes the protection. Which command sets that?
o: chown root:root /var/log/app-audit.log
Ownership doesn't stop root from editing or deleting.
chattr +i /var/log/app-audit.log
+i (immutable) blocks appending too, so logging would stop.
chmod 444 /var/log/app-audit.log
root ignores normal permission bits, and 444 also blocks appending by the app.
chattr +a /var/log/app-audit.log
Right. +a (append-only) lets data be added to the end but not changed or deleted. lsattr shows it.

q.q: You're hardening sshd_config on an internet-facing server. Every admin already logs in with an SSH key. Which TWO settings close the most common attack paths? (Choose two.)
o: UsePAM no
Turning off PAM breaks account checks and doesn't stop attacks.
PermitRootLogin no
Right. Attackers try root first; admins log in as themselves and use sudo.
PasswordAuthentication no
Right. With keys only, password guessing can't work.
X11Forwarding yes
That opens a feature most servers don't need; it doesn't harden anything.
PermitEmptyPasswords yes
That would allow accounts with no password to log in.

q.q: While troubleshooting, an admin wants SELinux to log denials but stop blocking them, only until the next reboot. Which command?
o: setenforce 0
Right. It switches to permissive mode now. The setting in /etc/selinux/config is used again at the next boot.
getenforce
getenforce only shows the current mode.
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
That changes one policy boolean, not the mode, and -P makes it permanent.
Set SELINUX=disabled in /etc/selinux/config
That's permanent, needs a reboot and disables logging too; re-enabling later needs a full relabel.

q.q: Policy says an account locks for 15 minutes after 5 failed logins. Which PAM module handles that on current RHEL-family systems?
o: pam_limits, configured in /etc/security/limits.conf
pam_limits sets resource limits like open files and processes.
pam_faillock, configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf
Right. pam_faillock counts failures and locks the account (deny=5, unlock_time=900).
pam_unix, using the PASS_MAX_DAYS line in /etc/login.defs
PASS_MAX_DAYS is password age, not failed-login lockout.
pam_motd, which shows a warning after a failed login
pam_motd shows the message of the day; it locks nothing.

q.q: Linux servers must accept Active Directory logins and still let users log in with cached credentials when the domain controller is unreachable. What fits?
o: Write a Polkit rule that trusts the domain controller
Polkit authorizes privileged actions on the host; it doesn't do domain logins.
Join the domain with realm join and use SSSD
Right. SSSD talks to AD through LDAP and Kerberos and caches credentials for offline logins.
Mount the domain controller's SYSVOL share over NFS
A file share doesn't authenticate anyone.
Create a matching local account on every server for every AD user
That doesn't use AD at all, and passwords would drift apart.

q.q: A user runs kinit and types their password once. What do they get that lets them reach Kerberos services without typing it again?
o: A new SSH key pair stored under ~/.ssh
Kerberos doesn't create SSH keys.
An X.509 certificate signed by the domain CA
That's PKI. Kerberos uses tickets.
A ticket-granting ticket (TGT)
Right. The TGT is used to request service tickets, so the password isn't sent again until it expires.
A one-time code that changes every 30 seconds
That describes TOTP, used for MFA.

q.q: You must record which user changes /etc/passwd and when, and search for it later. What do you set up?
o: An auditd watch rule on /etc/passwd, searched with ausearch
Right. auditd logs writes and attribute changes with the user (even after sudo) and time. Put the rule in /etc/audit/rules.d/ to keep it.
A cron job that copies /etc/passwd every hour and runs diff against the last copy
diff shows what changed, but not who changed it or exactly when.
chattr +i /etc/passwd so it can't change at all
That blocks legitimate changes like useradd and records nothing.
tail -f /var/log/messages in a screen session all day
/var/log/messages doesn't record file edits, and nobody can watch it all day.

q.q: On a firewalld server, HTTPS must be allowed now and after every reboot. Which commands do that?
o: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT, then service iptables save
Hand-added rules can be wiped when firewalld reloads, and they don't persist.
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https, then firewall-cmd --reload
Right. --permanent saves it to the config, and --reload loads the saved config into the running firewall.
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=443/udp, then --reload
HTTPS uses TCP 443; this opens UDP.
firewall-cmd --add-service=https
Without --permanent, the rule is gone after a reload or reboot.

q.q: On an Ubuntu server with ufw, SSH must be allowed only from the admin network 10.0.5.0/24. Which rule?
o: ufw allow from 10.0.5.0/24 to any port 22 proto tcp
Right. It allows TCP 22 only when the source is the admin subnet.
ufw allow 22/tcp
That allows SSH from everywhere.
ufw deny from 10.0.5.0/24 to any port 22
That blocks the admin network, the opposite.
ufw default allow incoming
That allows every port from everywhere.

q.q: A server's nftables input chain drops everything by default. It allows SSH in, but software updates now time out. Which missing rule is the most likely fix?
o: log prefix "DROP " drop
Logging drops helps you see the problem; it doesn't fix it.
ct state established,related accept
Right. A stateful rule lets replies to connections the server started (DNS answers, repo downloads) back in.
tcp dport 443 accept
That allows new inbound HTTPS to the server, not replies to its own outbound requests.
ct state new accept
That allows every new inbound connection, which defeats the firewall.

q.q: A Linux box routes between 10.1.0.0/24 and 10.2.0.0/24. Both interfaces are up, the firewall allows forwarding, but no traffic passes between the subnets. What is most likely missing?
o: A restart of NetworkManager on the router
Restarting the network doesn't change the forwarding setting.
IP forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward=1)
Right. By default the kernel doesn't pass packets between interfaces; this setting turns routing on.
A masquerade rule, because routing needs NAT
Routing between two private subnets doesn't need NAT.
A static route on the router pointing to itself
Both subnets are directly connected, so the router already has routes to them.

q.q:
These iptables rules were added in this order:
-A INPUT -j DROP
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
SSH is blocked. Why, and what's the fix?
o: Rules match top-down; insert the SSH rule first with -I
Right. iptables checks rules top-down, so the drop catches SSH before the accept rule is reached.
iptables reads rules bottom-up, so swap the policy to ACCEPT
Rules are read top-down; an ACCEPT policy would open everything.
The accept rule needs -m state --state NEW to match
The order is the problem; adding state matching won't help.
Port 22 must be written as ssh in the rule
Port numbers work fine; names are optional.

q.q: A kiosk account may run a few commands, but must not change directory, change PATH or redirect output into files. Which shell fits?
o: /bin/sh with a short HISTFILESIZE
sh is a normal shell with no restrictions.
rbash (restricted bash)
Right. rbash blocks cd, changing PATH, output redirection and running commands with a / in the name.
/usr/sbin/nologin
nologin refuses the login completely, so no commands run.
zsh with a long HISTSIZE
History size has nothing to do with restrictions.

q.q: Why should admins log in with their own accounts and use sudo instead of logging in as root?
o: sudo encrypts every command
sudo doesn't encrypt anything.
Commands run faster with sudo
Speed is the same either way.
Accountability and least privilege
Right. sudo records the real user for each command (accountability) and supports least privilege.
root can't log in with SSH keys
root can use keys; the issue is shared, untraceable logins.

q.q: Policy says new passwords need at least 14 characters. Where do you set that on a system using pam_pwquality?
o: minlen = 14 in /etc/security/pwquality.conf
Right. pam_pwquality checks new passwords against the rules in pwquality.conf.
PASS_WARN_AGE 14 in /etc/login.defs
That's how many days of warning before a password expires.
chage -M 14 for each user
-M sets maximum password age in days, not length.
Add 14 to the second field of /etc/shadow
That field holds the password hash; editing it breaks logins.

q.q: Which change actually adds a second factor to SSH logins?
o: Require 20-character passwords and change them every 30 days
That's still one factor: something you know.
Move SSH from port 22 to port 2222
Changing the port cuts noise but adds no factor.
An SSH key plus a one-time code from an authenticator app
Right. Two different factors: something you have (the private key) and a code from a device. sshd's AuthenticationMethods can require both.
Ask for the password twice at login with a PAM prompt
Two passwords are still the same factor.

q.q: Laptops that carry unit data could be lost. The whole data partition must be unreadable without a passphrase. What fits?
o: chmod 600 on every file on the partition
Permissions don't protect a disk read from another system.
Serve the files only over HTTPS
TLS protects data in transit, not a stolen disk.
Encrypt the partition with LUKS
Right. LUKS is full-disk encryption for data at rest; without the key, the disk is unreadable.
Compress the partition with gzip each night
Compression isn't encryption; anyone can uncompress it.

q.q: You downloaded a Linux ISO. How do you confirm it wasn't changed or corrupted?
o: Open it with base64 -d and look for errors
base64 decoding has nothing to do with integrity.
Run file on it and check it says ISO 9660
That confirms the format, not that the content is unchanged.
Compare its size in ls -l with the size on the website
Two different files can have the same size.
Compare its sha256sum with the vendor's signed list
Right. Matching SHA-256 hashes mean the file is identical; checking the signature on the list proves the list came from the vendor.

q.q: A vulnerability scan flags your SSH server for 3des-cbc ciphers and hmac-md5. What fixes the finding?
o: Allow only strong Ciphers and MACs in sshd_config
Right. Removing weak algorithms from the allowed lists stops clients from negotiating them.
Open TCP 22 in the firewall only to the scanner's address
That hides the finding from the scanner; the weakness stays.
Switch all users from passwords to SSH keys
Key login doesn't change which ciphers the connection uses.
Move SSH to another port so the scanner can't find it
The weak ciphers are still offered on the new port.

q.q: Why should an internal web server use a certificate from the organization's CA instead of a self-signed one?
o: Self-signed certificates expire 24 hours after they are made
You choose the expiry when you create one.
Self-signed certificates always use weaker encryption ciphers
The cipher strength is the same; trust is the problem.
Clients can verify it, so users aren't trained to click through warnings
Right. A self-signed cert can't be checked against a trusted CA. Users who learn to click past warnings won't notice a real man-in-the-middle.
Self-signed certificates can't be used with TLS 1.3 at all
TLS 1.3 works with them; browsers just can't trust them.

q.q: You must detect if anyone changes system binaries or files in /etc on a server. Which tool fits?
o: ClamAV
ClamAV looks for known malware signatures, not any change.
fail2ban
fail2ban bans IPs after repeated failed logins.
AIDE
Right. AIDE stores hashes and attributes in a baseline database (aide --init) and reports any difference on each check.
logrotate
logrotate rotates and compresses log files.

q.q: Servers with SSDs are being decommissioned and the drives reused elsewhere. Which method most reliably destroys the data?
o: A fresh filesystem on each drive with a quick mkfs.ext4 format
A format writes a new empty filesystem but leaves most old data in place.
rm -rf / followed by an empty trash
Deleting files only removes the directory entries; the data stays.
shred -n 3 on each file before deletion
On SSDs, shred can't reach blocks that wear leveling moved, so copies survive.
The drive's built-in secure erase, or destroy it
Right. SSD wear leveling keeps old copies of blocks where software overwrites can't reach; the drive's own erase handles them.

q.q: Policy says a legal warning must appear before anyone logs in over SSH. How do you set it?
o: Put the text in /etc/motd
motd is shown after a successful login, which is too late for a warning.
Put the text in /etc/hostname
That file sets the system's name.
Set Banner /etc/issue.net in sshd_config
Right. The Banner file (here /etc/issue.net, holding the warning text) is shown before authentication.
Put the text in the PS1 variable in /etc/bashrc
PS1 is the shell prompt, shown after login.

q.q: A developer added a third-party repo with gpgcheck=0 because the install failed with a key error. What should you do?
o: Leave it, since HTTPS already protects the download
HTTPS protects the transfer, not a repo that was compromised.
Leave it, but run dnf clean all after each install
Clearing the cache doesn't verify anything.
Set gpgcheck=0 on every repo so they match
That removes the protection everywhere.
Set gpgcheck=1 and import the vendor's real signing key
Right. Signature checks prove packages came from the vendor and weren't tampered with, which protects the software supply chain.

q.q: Auditors want proof that RHEL servers meet the DISA STIG, checked automatically. Which tool fits?
o: OpenSCAP (oscap) with the STIG profile
Right. oscap scans the system against a security profile and writes a pass or fail report for each rule.
tcpdump on the server's main interface
tcpdump captures traffic; it doesn't check settings.
nmap with the -A option against each server
nmap scans ports and services from outside; it doesn't check config against a STIG.
logwatch with the daily report option
logwatch summarizes logs; it doesn't check compliance.

q.q:
A script has the line: if [ $count -gt 10 ]; then
When count is empty it fails with "[: -gt: unary operator expected". What fixes it?
o: Change -gt to > so the shell compares the numbers as text instead
Inside [ ], > is a redirection that creates a file named 10.
Add set -e at the top of the script so the error is ignored
set -e makes the script stop on errors; it doesn't fix the test.
Quote the variable: [ "$count" -gt 10 ], or use [[ ]]
Right. Unquoted, an empty $count disappears and [ only sees "-gt 10". Quoted, it stays as an empty argument and the test gives a clean error or result.
Put the whole if statement inside $( ) so it runs in a subshell
A subshell has the same empty variable and fails the same way.

q.q: check.sh starts with #!/bin/bash and uses [[ ]]. ./check.sh works, but sh check.sh fails with "[[: not found". Why?
o: [[ ]] only works when the script is run with sudo or as the root user
[[ ]] is a bash feature with nothing to do with privileges.
The script is missing the execute bit, so sh falls back to a reduced mode
sh check.sh doesn't need the execute bit at all.
bash must be told about [[ with shopt -s extglob near the top of the file
extglob adds extra glob patterns; [[ is always built into bash.
sh ignores the #! line, and dash has no [[
Right. The #! line is used only when the file is run directly. Use ./check.sh or bash check.sh.

q.q: In a bash script, which variable holds the exit status of the last command, where 0 means success?
o: $0 is the name of the script itself.
$# is the number of arguments passed to the script.
Right. Check it right after the command, because the next command replaces it.
$! is the PID of the last background job.

q.q: hosts.txt has one entry per line, and some lines contain spaces ("web 01 primary"). Which loop handles each whole line safely?
o: while IFS= read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < hosts.txt
Right. read takes one full line at a time; IFS= keeps leading spaces and -r keeps backslashes.
for line in "hosts.txt"; do echo "$line"; done
That loops once over the literal word hosts.txt, not the file's lines.
while read line in hosts.txt; do echo "$line"; done
That isn't valid read syntax; the file has to come in through < redirection.
for line in $(cat hosts.txt); do echo "$line"; done
The unquoted $(cat) splits on every space, so "web 01 primary" becomes three items.

q.q: Which test is true only when $name is "vm-" followed by one or more digits, like vm-042?
o: With = the right side is a glob pattern, so ^ and + are taken literally.
Right. =~ compares against an extended regular expression; ^ and $ anchor the whole string.
Without anchors it also matches things like old-vm-1x.
[ $name == vm-* ]
[ ] does no pattern matching: it compares with the literal text vm-* (or with file names, if the unquoted glob expands).

q.q: Why should a Python admin script use a virtual environment instead of sudo pip install for its packages?
o: A venv encrypts the installed packages on disk
venvs are plain folders and don't encrypt anything.
sudo pip can break the OS's own Python tools
Right. Many system tools use the distro's Python. A venv gives each project its own packages without touching them.
A venv compiles the script to machine code so it runs faster
venvs don't compile anything; speed is the same.
pip can't install anything as root, so a venv is the only way
pip can install as root; the problem is what it overwrites.

q.q: A Python script must run df -h and keep its output in a variable. Which built-in module is meant for that?
o: subprocess
Right. subprocess.run(["df", "-h"], capture_output=True, text=True) runs the program and captures its output and exit code.
json
json reads and writes JSON; it doesn't run commands.
os.path
os.path joins and inspects paths; it doesn't run commands.
sys.argv
sys.argv holds the arguments passed to your script.

q.q: Which function definition follows PEP 8 style?
o: def disk-usage(path):  (body indented 2 spaces)
A hyphen isn't allowed in a Python name at all.
def DiskUsage(Path):  (body indented 4 spaces)
CapWords is for class names, not functions or arguments.
def diskUsage(path):  (body indented with one tab)
camelCase isn't PEP 8 style, and PEP 8 prefers spaces over tabs.
def disk_usage(path):  (body indented 4 spaces)
Right. PEP 8 uses lowercase_with_underscores for function and variable names and 4-space indents.

q.q: Your script works in your venv. A teammate needs the exact same package versions. What do you share?
o: The output of pip show for the main package only
That shows one package, not every dependency and version.
The output of pip list pasted into a chat message
pip list isn't in a format pip can install from.
The whole .venv folder zipped and emailed to the teammate
venvs contain absolute paths and break when moved.
A requirements.txt made with pip freeze
Right. pip freeze lists every installed package with its exact version; they run pip install -r requirements.txt.

q.q:
A script is run as: python3 cleanup.py /var/log/app 7
Inside the script, what is sys.argv[1]?
o: "python3"
The interpreter isn't in sys.argv.
"cleanup.py"
That's sys.argv[0].
"/var/log/app"
Right. sys.argv[0] is the script name, so sys.argv[1] is the first argument. Every item is a string.
7, as an integer
That's sys.argv[2], and it's the string "7" until you convert it.

q.q: You changed deploy.sh but haven't staged or committed it. You want to throw away your changes and get the last committed version back. Which command?
o: git rm deploy.sh
That deletes the file and stages the deletion.
git reset --hard HEAD~1
That also throws away your last commit and every other uncommitted change.
git revert deploy.sh
revert makes a new commit that undoes an earlier commit; it takes a commit, not a file.
git restore deploy.sh
Right. git restore resets the file in your working folder to the committed version (older Git: git checkout -- deploy.sh).

q.q: A bad commit was already pushed to the shared main branch and teammates have pulled it. What is the safe way to undo it?
o: git commit --amend, then git push --force
That also rewrites shared history and only changes the latest commit.
git revert <commit>, then push
Right. revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody's history is rewritten.
Delete the remote repository and push a fresh copy
That destroys history for everyone.
git reset --hard <commit>~1, then git push --force
Force-pushing rewrites shared history and breaks your teammates' copies.

q.q: You're halfway through a change on a feature branch when you must fix something on main. You don't want to commit unfinished work. What do you do?
o: git fetch, which moves your changes to the remote safely
fetch downloads from the remote; it doesn't save your work.
git reset --hard, switch to main, then redo your work later
That throws your unfinished work away.
git checkout main --force so the changes come along to main
--force throws away local changes that conflict.
git stash, switch to main, fix it, then switch back and git stash pop
Right. stash saves uncommitted changes and cleans the folder; pop brings them back.

q.q: You added .env (which holds API keys) to .gitignore, but git status still shows changes to .env. Why?
o: It's already tracked; run git rm --cached .env
Right. .gitignore only affects untracked files, and once a file is committed Git keeps tracking it. Also treat the keys as leaked and rotate them, since they're in history.
Git reads .gitignore only from the home directory, not the repo
Git reads .gitignore files inside the repo.
.gitignore only works after the next git push to the remote
.gitignore works locally right away for untracked files.
.gitignore needs a /*.env wildcard pattern, not a plain file name
A plain name matches; the problem is that the file is already tracked.

q.q: You want to see what teammates pushed to origin/main without changing your local branch or files. Which command comes first?
o: git merge
merge changes your branch and uses what was last fetched.
git pull
pull fetches and then merges into your branch, changing your files.
git fetch
Right. fetch downloads new commits without merging. Then compare with git log HEAD..origin/main.
git push
push sends your commits; it doesn't download theirs.

q.q: An AI assistant gives you a one-liner with rm -rf to clean old logs. What is the responsible next step?
o: Run it right away, since the AI has already tested the command
AI assistants don't run or test your commands.
Run it with sudo so it can't fail halfway through the cleanup
sudo makes a wrong command do more damage, not less.
Understand it, then test it in a lab first
Right. AI can be confidently wrong. A small path or quoting error in rm -rf can delete the wrong data.
Add it to root's crontab so it runs every night unattended
That repeats an untested command with no one watching.

q.q: You want a public AI chatbot's help with a failing service log. What is the best practice?
o: Paste the server's /etc/shadow too so it can check user accounts
Password hashes are secrets and must never be shared.
Paste the full log as-is; the chatbot deletes it after the session
You can't count on that, and the log can contain secrets.
Paste your SSH private key so it can test logging in for you
A private key gives full access to whoever has it.
Remove hostnames, IP addresses, usernames, keys and passwords before pasting
Right. Anything you paste may be stored or seen by others. Share only what's needed, and never secrets or CUI.

q.q: Which prompt is most likely to get a useful answer from an AI assistant?
o: "Is Linux better than Windows for servers?"
It's an opinion question, not your problem.
"On Rocky Linux 9, nginx won't start after I changed listen to 8081. Here's the journalctl output: ... What's the likely cause?"
Right. Good prompts give the system, the goal, what changed and the real error.
"Write me a Linux server"
The goal is too vague to give a useful answer.
"nginx broken, fix it"
There's no system, error or context to work from.

q.q: An AI assistant tells you to run "systemctl restart --all-units nginx". The command errors out. What is the most likely explanation, and what should you do?
o: Your systemd version is too old, so upgrade the whole OS first
Jumping to an upgrade wastes time when the option may not exist at all.
The shell is blocking the command, so run it inside sudo bash -c
The error comes from systemctl not knowing the option.
nginx is masked, so unmask it and run the same command again
Masking gives a different error; this one is about the option.
The AI made up an option; check man systemctl or the official docs
Right. AI can invent (hallucinate) commands and options that look real. The man page is the source of truth.

q.q: Which statement describes Ansible?
o: It needs a SQL database on every managed host to store that host's state
Managed hosts need only SSH and Python.
It compiles shell scripts into binaries that run faster on each managed host
Ansible doesn't compile anything.
Agentless: it pushes YAML playbooks over SSH
Right. Ansible is agentless: the control node connects over SSH and runs tasks.
An agent on every host pulls its config from a master server every 30 minutes
That describes Puppet's usual pull model.

q.q: An Ansible playbook ensures nginx is installed and running. You run it twice. On the second run nothing changes. What property is this?
o: Immutability
Immutable infrastructure means replacing systems instead of changing them.
Idempotence
Right. Running the same automation again leaves an already-correct system unchanged, so it's safe to rerun.
Orchestration
Orchestration coordinates steps across many systems.
Elasticity
Elasticity is scaling resources up and down with demand.

q.q: What is a key benefit of infrastructure as code (IaC) tools like OpenTofu or Ansible?
o: It records your clicks in the cloud console and plays them back later
IaC is written definitions, not recorded clicks.
It makes each server's CPU run faster under heavy production load
IaC doesn't change hardware performance.
Setups are versioned, reviewed and repeatable
Right. Code can be reviewed, tracked in Git and rerun, which avoids hand-made differences (drift) between servers.
Once infrastructure is written as code, it never needs any testing
IaC changes still need testing, ideally in a pipeline.

q.q: You must install RHEL on 50 new servers, all the same, with nobody at the keyboard. What fits?
o: An Ansible playbook run against the blank servers to install the OS
Ansible needs a running OS with SSH, so it can't install onto blank disks.
Install one server by hand and give the team a checklist for the rest
That's still 49 manual installs.
A Kickstart file used with network (PXE) installs
Right. Kickstart answers every installer question automatically (preseed and cloud-init do similar jobs).
dd one installed disk onto the other 49 servers by hand
Hand cloning is slow, and every copy has the same IDs and keys.

q.q: In a CI/CD pipeline, what normally happens when a developer pushes a change?
o: A person copies the files to the server by hand over FTP
That's a manual process, not CI/CD.
It goes straight to production, then the tests run afterward
Testing after deployment means users find the bugs first.
Builds and tests run; it deploys only if they pass
Right. CI catches problems early, and CD deploys only changes that passed.
The servers reboot so they pick up the new code from Git
Pipelines deploy code; rebooting doesn't.

q.q: Users get "No space left on device" when they create files in /var. df -h shows /var at 41%. What should you check next?
o: lsblk, because the disk may have been removed while mounted
A removed disk gives I/O errors, not a full-device error.
df -i, because the filesystem may be out of inodes
Right. Every file uses an inode. Millions of tiny files (session or cache files) can use up all the inodes while space is still free.
fdisk -l, because the partition table may have been damaged
A damaged partition table wouldn't show a healthy 41%.
free -h, because the server may be out of RAM and swap
Memory errors don't come back as "No space left on device".

q.q: df -h shows / at 100% used, but du -sh on every top-level folder adds up to only half the disk. What is a common cause?
o: A deleted file is still held open by a running process
Right. Its space isn't freed until the process closes it. lsof +L1 lists such files; restarting the process frees the space.
The filesystem journal is using half the disk
A journal is small and fixed in size.
du can't read compressed files, so it counts them as half their size
du counts real disk usage either way.
df counts in GiB but du counts in GB, so the totals differ
Both use the same units with -h; that couldn't explain half the disk.

q.q: You added a line to /etc/fstab for a USB backup disk. The disk wasn't attached at the next boot, and the server dropped to emergency mode. What is the right fix?
o: Fix the fstab line (add nofail), then reboot
Right. systemd treats a missing fstab mount as a failure unless nofail is set. A removable disk should always have nofail.
Rebuild the initramfs with dracut -f from the emergency shell
The initramfs isn't involved in mounting the backup disk.
Boot from a rescue USB and reinstall GRUB to the boot disk
GRUB worked fine; the boot stopped at a mount.
Run fsck on the root filesystem from the emergency shell
The root filesystem isn't damaged; a missing disk is the issue.

q.q: An ext4 filesystem on /data reports errors in the logs. What is the right way to run a repair?
o: Run mkfs.ext4 on the device to rebuild its metadata
mkfs creates a new empty filesystem and erases the data.
Run xfs_repair on the /data device
xfs_repair is for XFS, not ext4.
Run fsck on /data while it stays mounted and in use
fsck on a mounted filesystem can make the damage worse.
Unmount /data (or use rescue mode), then run e2fsck on it
Right. Repairing a mounted filesystem can corrupt it further, because the system keeps writing to it during the check.

q.q: After a kernel update a RHEL server has driver problems. You need it to keep booting the previous kernel by default while you investigate. Which command?
o: Delete the new kernel's files from /boot by hand
That leaves broken boot entries and package records.
grubby --set-default /boot/vmlinuz-<previous version>
Right. grubby changes the default boot entry without removing the new kernel.
dnf downgrade glibc to the previous version
glibc is a library, not the kernel.
Set GRUB_TIMEOUT=30 in /etc/default/grub
A longer menu wait doesn't change the default kernel.

q.q:
ip link shows:
eth0: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500 state DOWN
What is the problem?
o: The interface is disabled; run ip link set eth0 up to turn it on
UP in the flags shows it's already enabled.
The MTU is too small and needs to be raised to 9000
1500 is normal, and MTU doesn't cause NO-CARRIER.
No physical link: check the cable or switch port
Right. UP means the admin enabled it; NO-CARRIER means nothing is connected at the other end (for a VM, check the virtual NIC is connected).
DHCP failed to give it an address
Without a link, DHCP can't even start. Fix the link first.

q.q: A server can ping 8.8.8.8 but "ping updates.example.com" says "Temporary failure in name resolution". Where do you look first?
o: The ARP table
ARP is local addressing and works since outside pings succeed.
The default gateway
Pinging an outside IP already worked, so routing is fine.
The DNS settings
Right. Reaching an IP proves routing works. Failing on a name points to DNS: check /etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl status.
The interface MTU
Those would affect all traffic, not only names.

q.q:
A server can reach other hosts on its own subnet, 10.0.4.0/24, but nothing outside it. ip route shows only:
10.0.4.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.4.15
What is missing?
o: An ARP entry for each remote host
ARP is only used on the local subnet.
A second IP address on eth0 in the remote subnet
Remote networks are reached through a gateway, not extra addresses.
A DNS server in /etc/resolv.conf
DNS isn't needed to reach an IP address on another network.
A default route (for example default via 10.0.4.1)
Right. Without a default route, the server doesn't know where to send traffic for other networks.

q.q:
A web app runs and curl http://localhost:8080 works on the server, but other machines get "connection refused". ss -tlnp shows:
LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("java",pid=2210))
What is the cause?
o: Another program is already using port 8080
ss shows java is the one listening on it.
It listens only on 127.0.0.1
Right. Loopback accepts local connections only. Set the app's bind or listen address to 0.0.0.0 or the server's IP, then restart it.
DNS has the wrong IP address for the server's name
The clients reached the server and were refused, so DNS worked.
The host firewall is dropping port 8080 from other machines
A firewall drop usually causes a timeout, and the loopback-only bind already explains it.

q.q: After a firewall change, clients time out (no reply at all) connecting to TCP 443 on a server. ss shows nginx listening on 0.0.0.0:443 and curl works locally. What is most likely?
o: The TLS certificate expired at the same time
An expired certificate gives a browser warning, not a timeout.
nginx crashed after the change and needs to be started again
ss shows it's listening and local curl works.
nginx is bound to the loopback address only
0.0.0.0 means every address.
The host firewall drops inbound 443
Right. A timeout with a working local listener points to something silently dropping packets, like a firewall rule.

q.q: You moved site files with mv from /home/dev/site to /var/www/html. Apache returns 403. Permissions look right, and ausearch shows an AVC denial for httpd. What is the fix?
o: setenforce 0, then set SELINUX=disabled for good
That turns off a security layer instead of fixing one wrong label.
restorecon -Rv /var/www/html
Right. mv keeps the old SELinux label (user_home_t). restorecon applies the correct label (httpd_sys_content_t) for that path.
chmod -R 777 /var/www/html
Permissions were fine, and 777 lets anyone change the site.
chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html
Ownership wasn't the problem; the SELinux label was.

q.q: You changed httpd to listen on TCP 8081. It won't start, and the log shows SELinux denied the bind. What is the correct fix?
o: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8081/tcp, then reload
You'll also need this for clients, but it doesn't fix the SELinux denial.
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8081
Right. SELinux only allows httpd on ports labeled http_port_t; this adds 8081 to that label.
chcon -t http_port_t /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
That relabels the config file, not the port.
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
That boolean allows outbound connections from httpd, not binding a new port.

q.q: alice's SSH key login fails and falls back to a password prompt. The server log shows "Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/alice/.ssh". What is the fix?
o: Set the modes to 777 so sshd can always read the files
Open modes are exactly what sshd refuses.
Generate a new key pair for alice and try again
The key isn't the problem; the folder permissions are.
Set ~/.ssh to 700 and authorized_keys to 600
Right. sshd refuses keys if others could change the files (StrictModes). Both must also be owned by alice.
Set PubkeyAuthentication no in sshd_config
That turns key login off completely.

q.q: Users report certificate errors on an internal HTTPS site. Which command checks the server's certificate dates from the command line?
o: ssh-keygen -l -f /etc/pki/tls/certs/intranet.pem
ssh-keygen works with SSH keys, not X.509 certificates.
dig intranet TXT +short and read the expiry line
DNS TXT records don't hold the certificate.
curl -I http://intranet and check the date header
http:// doesn't use TLS, and the Date header is just the server's clock.
openssl s_client -connect intranet:443 </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
Right. s_client fetches the live certificate and x509 -dates prints notBefore and notAfter.

q.q: ls -l /tmp/setup.sh shows -rwxr-xr-x and you own it, but ./setup.sh says "Permission denied". mount shows /tmp with options rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec. Why?
o: /tmp is full and the kernel can't load the script
A full disk gives a different error, and the file already exists.
The SUID bit is missing, so the shell won't run it
Scripts don't need SUID to run.
The execute bit is missing for the group, so chmod g+x fixes it
You own the file, and the owner has x.
/tmp is mounted noexec, so nothing there can be run directly
Right. noexec is a common hardening setting for /tmp. Move the script somewhere else, or review it and run it with bash setup.sh.

q.q: top shows a load average of 12 on a 4-core server, but %us is only 5. The %wa (I/O wait) value is 70. What is the bottleneck?
o: The network
Network waits don't show up as %wa.
The CPU
%us is low, so the CPUs aren't busy computing.
Memory
Low free RAM alone is normal; nothing here points to memory.
Disk I/O
Right. High wa means the CPUs are idle while waiting for disk, and those waiting processes count toward load. Check iostat -x or iotop.

q.q: free -h shows only 300 MiB free, but buff/cache is 12 GiB and available is 11 GiB. The server runs fine. What does this mean?
o: Cache needs to be cleared every hour with drop_caches
Dropping caches hurts performance and solves nothing.
There's a memory leak, so the server should be restarted
The cache isn't a leak; it's freed on demand.
Nothing; Linux uses spare RAM for cache
Right. The cache is given back when apps need it. "available" is the number that matters.
The swap partition is too small and must be enlarged
Swap isn't even mentioned, and 11 GiB is available.

q.q: dmesg shows: "Out of memory: Killed process 4120 (java) total-vm:9100000kB". What happened?
o: java crashed with a bug and the kernel only logged it afterward
The message says the kernel killed it.
SELinux blocked java from using more memory than allowed
SELinux denials appear as AVC messages, not OOM kills.
The disk filled up, so the kernel stopped the biggest writer
Full disks don't trigger the OOM killer.
RAM ran out and the OOM killer ended java
Right. The OOM killer picks a process to free memory. Fix it by limiting the app's memory, adding RAM or finding a leak.

q.q: uptime shows: load average: 0.50, 2.10, 6.80. What does this tell you?
o: The server has three CPUs, each at a different load
The numbers are time windows, not CPUs.
The load is 6.80% of the server's capacity
Load is the number of running or waiting tasks, not a percentage.
The load is rising quickly and will get worse
The newest number (1 minute) is the smallest, so it's falling.
The load was high earlier and is dropping now
Right. The three numbers are the 1-, 5- and 15-minute averages. A low first number means it's calmer now.

q.q: A busy web app logs "Too many open files" under load. The server has plenty of RAM and CPU. What should you raise?
o: The app's open-files limit (nofile)
Right. Each connection and file uses a file descriptor, and the default per-process limit is often 1024. Raise it with LimitNOFILE= in the systemd unit.
The swap size in /etc/fstab
Swap doesn't affect file descriptor limits.
The app's nice value, to give it more CPU
Priority doesn't change file descriptor limits.
The number of inodes on the root filesystem
Inodes count files on disk, not files a process has open.

q.q: In a pull-based monitoring setup like Prometheus with node_exporter, how is the data collected?
o: Each host emails a report to the monitoring team every night
That's neither real-time nor how metrics are collected.
The monitoring server logs into each host over SSH to run top
Exporters serve metrics; the server doesn't need SSH.
Each host writes its metrics into a shared NFS folder
Exporters serve metrics over HTTP; they don't write to shares.
The server scrapes each host's exporter on a schedule
Right. In the pull model the server scrapes each target. In a push model, agents send data to the server.

q.q: The web service's process keeps running, but the site returns errors to users. Which check would catch this?
o: An HTTP check that expects a 200 response
Right. Checking what users actually get catches failures that a process check misses.
A check that the nginx process ID still exists
The process is running, so this check stays green.
A disk usage check on the web root folder
Disk space doesn't show whether pages work.
A ping check to the server's IP address
The server answers pings even while the site is broken.

q.q: A CPU alert fires and clears every few minutes as usage bounces around 80%. The team is starting to ignore it. What is the best fix?
o: Send the alert to more people so someone always responds
More noise to more people makes alert fatigue worse.
Lower the threshold to 60% so it fires earlier
That makes it fire even more often.
Turn the CPU alert off, since the team ignores it anyway
That leaves you blind when a real problem starts.
Alert only if it stays high for a set time
Right. A duration (or separate fire and clear levels) stops flapping, so each alert means something.

q.q: All servers must forward every syslog message to loghost.corp.local over TCP so messages aren't silently lost. Which rsyslog line does that?
o: *.* :omusrmsg:*
That writes messages to the terminals of logged-in users.
*.* @@loghost.corp.local:514
Right. @@ means TCP, which notices dropped connections. A single @ means UDP.
*.* /var/log/loghost.corp.local
That writes to a local file with that name.
*.* @loghost.corp.local:514
A single @ sends over UDP, which can drop messages without notice.

q.title: Undo a bad commit that is already on shared main
q.scenario: A teammate pushed a commit to the shared main branch of the team's Ansible repo and it breaks the nightly run. Other people have already pulled it. Build the safe steps that undo it without rewriting shared history. Put the needed steps in order and leave out the risky ones.
q.ticket: Repo: ansible-infra, branch main. The remote is named origin. You do not yet know the id of the bad commit.

rules.why: Brings your copy up to date. If someone pushed since you last pulled, git rejects your push, so you start from the newest main.
Lists recent commits with short ids and messages, so you can find the id of the bad commit.
Creates a new commit that undoes the bad one. History stays intact, so people who already pulled the bad commit can pull the fix normally.
Sends the revert commit to the shared branch so everyone gets the fix.

This moves only your own copy back one commit and discards work. The bad commit is still on the server and in teammates' copies, and if more than one commit was added since, you could drop the wrong one.
A force push overwrites shared history. Teammates who already pulled the bad commit end up with histories that no longer match, and other people's commits can be lost.
Amend rewrites your latest commit. The bad commit belongs to a teammate and is already pushed, so amending does not undo it and would also rewrite shared history.
Interactive rebase rewrites commits, and a rewritten branch would need a force push. Revert is the safe choice for work that others already have.

before.why: Pull first so the teammate's bad commit is in your copy; otherwise git log will not show it and git revert cannot find it.
You need the commit id from the log before you can tell git revert which commit to undo.

last.why: The push sends the finished revert commit. Anything done after it would not reach the shared branch.

q.title: Place the layers of a new /data volume on LVM
q.scenario: You are adding a new disk, /dev/sdb, and want /data to be able to grow later by adding more disks. Place each layer of the LVM stack, from the raw disk up to the mount point.

devs.name: Partition /dev/sdb1
devs.why: Most admins first make one partition (type Linux LVM) so other tools see the disk is in use. pvcreate can also use the whole disk.

devs.name: Physical volume (PV)
devs.why: pvcreate marks the partition for LVM. A PV is the building block that a volume group collects.

devs.name: Volume group (VG)
devs.why: vgcreate gathers one or more PVs into a pool. Adding a disk later (vgextend) makes the pool bigger.

devs.name: Logical volume (LV)
devs.why: lvcreate cuts a piece out of the pool. An LV can later be grown with lvextend.

devs.name: XFS filesystem
devs.why: mkfs.xfs puts a filesystem on the LV so it can be mounted at /data. Without it the LV has no files or folders.

devs.name: Swap area (mkswap)
devs.why: Swap is virtual memory on disk. It would use a different LV, not the layer that holds /data.

devs.name: mdadm RAID 1 (md0)
devs.why: Software RAID (mdadm) is a separate layer, not part of LVM, and RAID 1 needs at least two disks. Only one new disk is being added.

devs.name: Snapshot of the LV
devs.why: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy taken from an existing LV. It sits beside the LV and is not part of the chain from disk to mount point.
